title: Defending against Backdoor Attacks via Module Switching
claim: Swapping modules between two compromised models breaks each model's learned shortcut, so the combined model no longer carries either backdoor.
layout: 3 zones left-to-right: two stacked source models, central shield, combined model
description: A legend at the top maps a blue line to backdoor shortcut A and a red line to backdoor shortcut B. At left, two stacked square panels show Model A (light blue) and Model B (light pink). Each panel is split by a vertical divider, and a wavy shortcut curve runs from Input to Output. The curve in A is blue and the curve in B is red. A magenta dot marks the junction in A and a yellow dot marks the junction in B. In the center, a dashed vertical line passes through a shield icon. A gray 'Module-Switching' label sits above the shield. A red arrow enters the shield from the left and a blue arrow leaves it to the right. At right, the Combined Model (A & B) panel has a pink left half and a blue right half. The red curve on the left half and the blue curve on the right half no longer connect, and the magenta and yellow dots are offset. A gray box below reads 'Backdoor shortcuts are disrupted.'
caption: An illustration of \ourmethod. By switching weight modules between compromised models (left), the spurious correlations (shortcuts) learned from backdoored tasks are disrupted in the combined model (right).
abstract: Backdoor attacks pose a serious threat to deep neural networks (DNNs), allowing adversaries to implant triggers for hidden behaviors in inference. Defending against such vulnerabilities is especially difficult in the post-training setting, since end-users lack training data or prior knowledge of the attacks. Model merging offers a cost-effective defense; however, latest methods like weight averaging (WAG) provide reasonable protection when multiple homologous models are available, but are less effective with fewer models and place heavy demands on defenders. We propose a module-switching defense (MSD) for disrupting backdoor shortcuts. We first validate its theoretical rationale and empirical effectiveness on two-layer networks, showing its capability of achieving higher backdoor divergence than WAG, and preserving utility. For deep models, we evaluate MSD on Transformer and CNN architectures and design an evolutionary algorithm to optimize fusion strategies with selective mechanisms to identify the most effective combinations. Experiments show that MSD achieves stronger defense with fewer models in practical settings, and even under an underexplored case of collusive attacks among multiple models--where some models share the same backdoors--switching strategies by MSD deliver superior robustness against diverse attacks. Code is available at https://github.com/weijun-l/module-switching-defense.
